rv.q: It’s eye-opening, generous and brilliantly inventive.
The hope and anxiety, the immaturity and precocious wisdom, plus the hormonal agony and ecstasy of today’s teens is entertainingly and stirringly on view in Our Generation.
Overall this is a terrific piece of work.
Alecky Blythe’s latest verbatim drama fizzes with the energy of its sources.
At three hours 40 minutes with two intervals, this is a baggy, vivacious first draft, in need of cutting.
Appealing as these kids are, Our Generation goes nowhere new thematically or dramatically.

While Our Generation is engrossing and sensitively curated, it lacks depth – instead sailing along on the inherent charisma of the teenagers involved, hoping that profundity will arise out of the banality of day to day life.
But their reflections are too mundane; the breezy, chatty tone needs far more variation.
But gosh it's boring. Patronising too.
Director Daniel Evans makes this mini-epic brim with the buoyancy and flair that have characterised his work over the years.
It makes a long evening but it so engages that you don’t notice the time pass.
For those who have the temperament to sit through its long-running time, you’ll be treated to an extraordinarily original and boundary-pushing piece of theatre.

Blythe has made us care about these people, slowly using this anthology of scenes to create audience investment in them and their lives with comedy often the entry point for recognition, understanding and empathy.
But as a piece of theatre, it is heavy going, its sheer ambition also its greatest weakness.

cn.t: Blythe's ambitious verbatim portrait of British teenagers earns praise for its authenticity and strong performances, but critics split on whether its nearly four-hour runtime justifies the material.
